content: ExxonMobil (XOM) is trading at $167.23, slightly above its $166.24 pivot but still below its 20-day and 26-day moving averages. The tape is weak: RSI is below 40, MACD momentum is flat-to-bearish, ... ExxonMobil (XOM) is sitting at $167.23, with a 24-hour gain of 0.77%, but the broader setup still looks technically fragile. The stock is trading under the 20-day SMA of $176.03 and the 26-day EMA of $172.37, while the 7-day SMA at $166.21 is only slightly below spot. That tells you the bounce is still short-term in nature rather than a clean trend reversal. The key intraday structure is centered around a pivot point of $166.24, with immediate support at $163.47 and stronger support at $159.72. On the upside, immediate resistance sits at $169.99, with stronger resistance at $172.76. The Bollinger middle band at $176.03 and lower band at $158.36 frame the current range, and the %B reading of 0.2510 suggests price is still occupying the lower part of that band structure. The daily RSI at 38.61 is still in neutral territory, but it is weak neutral, not a sign of strength. MACD is negative at -2.4192, with the signal line matching it and the histogram flat at 0.0000. That combination usually points to a market that has stopped accelerating lower, but has not yet proven that buyers are taking control. Stochastic readings are also subdued, with %K at 22.03 and %D at 17.63. That keeps the short-term picture tilted to the downside, even if the stock is no longer in an outright oversold collapse. Binance perpetual futures data does not give a simple one-way read. Funding is negative at -0.0576%, which means shorts are paying longs, but that alone does not confirm a durable bullish setup. It mainly shows positioning is skewed enough that long holders are being compensated. Open interest rose 11.21% over 24 hours to 3,003.64 contracts, with an open interest value of $592,635. That is a meaningful build in exposure, but it needs confirmation from price follow-through. So far, the market is showing a low-volume bounce, with volume at 0.23x versus the 5-day average. In plain terms: participation is light, and rallies built on light volume tend to be easier to fade. The long/short ratios lean slightly long. Binance global accounts are 53.4% long versus 46.6% short, and top-trader accounts are 55.1% long versus 44.9% short. But taker flow is the cleaner short-term read: the taker buy/sell ratio is 0.8676, with buy volume of 117 versus sell volume of 135, which points to more aggressive selling pressure in the latest 1-hour window. The freshest analyst marks in the evidence are not especially supportive. Sergey Pigarev of Freedom Broker raised the price target to $162 from $142 while keeping a Hold rating on November 6, 2026. DZ Bank was more cautious on November 5, downgrading ExxonMobil from Hold to Sell and setting a $170 target. Those targets matter because they bracket the stock tightly around the current market price. XOM at $167.23 is already above the Freedom Broker target and just below the DZ Bank target, which underscores how limited the near-term upside case looks from this set of estimates alone. If ExxonMobil can reclaim $169.99 and then push through $172.76, the burden shifts back to the bulls and opens the door toward the $176.03 area where the 20-day average and Bollinger middle band sit. If instead $163.47 gives way, the market is likely to test $159.72, with $158.36 as the next technical reference from the lower Bollinger band. The current read is not a clean bearish breakdown, but it is also not a convincing trend reversal. Price is holding above nearby support, yet momentum, volume, and taker flow still argue that XOM needs stronger demand before the chart can reset higher. title: Chevron Q3 Earnings Surge on Strong Refining: Is the Stock a Buy Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron CorporationCVX posted a sharp increase in third-quarter 2026 earnings, as stronger refining margins and record U.S. refinery throughput helped lift profitability. The energy giant earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per diluted share, compared with $3.54 billion, or $1.82, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings reached $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. The strong results were accompanied by healthy cash generation, rising earnings estimates and continued shareholder returns. Chevron has also delivered better year-to-date share-price performance than integrated energy peers ExxonMobil Holdings CorporationXOM and Shell plc SHEL. Let's examine the factors supporting its investment case. Chevron's downstream business played a major role in its third-quarter earnings growth. The segment generated $4.93 billion in earnings, up from $1.14 billion a year earlier, benefiting from stronger refining margins and reliable operations. This improvement was particularly noticeable in the United States, where downstream earnings jumped to $3.59 billion from $638 million in the year-ago quarter. U.S. refinery crude throughput reached a record 1.09 million barrels per day, with capacity utilization approaching 98%. Chevron is also making better use of its existing refining infrastructure. At the Pasadena refinery, the company increased processing capacity by approximately 15% through debottlenecking improvements, adding throughput capacity at relatively little cost. These initiatives highlight Chevron's focus on getting more value from its assets. Much like ExxonMobil and Shell, Chevron's integrated operations allow it to participate across the energy value chain, with refining serving as an important contributor to overall earnings. Analysts have become more optimistic about Chevron's earnings outlook, as reflected in upward revisions of the consensus estimates. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate trend for Chevron's 2026 earnings has risen 12.90%, while the same for 2027 has increased 22.85%. ExxonMobil's earnings estimates for 2026 and 2027 have increased 12.60% and 15.45%, respectively. Shell has recorded corresponding increases of 13.69% and 10.64%. While all three companies have seen upward revisions, Chevron stands out for 2027, with its estimate increasing more sharply than those of both peers. The stronger revisions suggest growing confidence in Chevron's ability to sustain earnings performance. Its refining operations, disciplined spending and expanding production opportunities provide several potential drivers of future profitability. Chevron's valuation also merits attention. The stock trades at 11.76 times forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E), slightly below ExxonMobil's multiple of 12.13 times. Shell, meanwhile, trades at 8.91 times. Although Chevron commands a premium over Shell, the modest discount to ExxonMobil offers an interesting comparison, particularly given its recent earnings performance and improving analyst expectations. Chevron's combination of reliable operations, substantial cash generation and shareholder distributions provides support for its valuation. For investors looking to gain exposure to a diversified energy producer, CVX offers an appealing mix of earnings potential and financial stability. Chevron has also performed well in the stock market. Shares of CVX have gained approximately 39.8% year to date, ahead of ExxonMobil's 38.4% increase and Shell's 33.2% rise. That gives Chevron a lead of 1.4 percentage points over ExxonMobil and 6.6 percentage points over Shell. The share-price gains have come alongside strong refining profitability, solid cash generation and improving earnings expectations. These developments have helped strengthen Chevron's standing among major integrated energy companies. With analysts continuing to raise their earnings estimates, Chevron has additional fundamental support for its investment outlook. Chevron's cash-generating ability remains a key attraction. The company generated $16 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter, while adjusted free cash flow reached $14.2 billion. The company returned $6 billion to its shareholders, comprising $3.5 billion in dividends and $2.5 billion in share repurchases. Chevron also reduced total debt by approximately $3.5 billion during the quarter, further strengthening its balance sheet. Its production operations continue to deliver encouraging results. U.S. output exceeded 2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Production in the Permian Basin remained around 1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the sixth straight quarter. Chevron is also positioning itself for future expansion. Its Venezuelan joint ventures are targeting approximately 600,000 barrels per day of gross production by 2031, creating another potential avenue for growth. Together, steady production, capital discipline and strategic investments provide a strong foundation for Chevron's longer-term prospects. Chevron's third-quarter results offer several reasons for optimism. Strong refining profitability, record U.S. crude throughput and substantial cash generation demonstrate the company's ability to make the most of its integrated operations. Rising earnings estimates, a competitive valuation relative to ExxonMobil and better year-to-date share-price performance than both XOM and SHEL further strengthen the investment case. Chevron's commitment to shareholder returns and its plans to expand production add to the positives. With a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), CVX looks attractive for investors seeking exposure to the integrated energy industry. Its combination of solid earnings, healthy cash flow and long-term growth opportunities makes the stock worth considering for an investment portfolio. title: Exxon, Chevron, and Shell Just Reported. Here's What Each One Said About Where Oil Goes Next. - The Motley Fool
content: Uncertainty is the main issue in the oil market, but that doesn't mean that these integrated energy giants aren't making plans. ExxonMobil (XOM +1.84%), Shell (SHEL +0.71%), and Chevron (CVX +1.44%) have their fingers on the pulse of the global energy market. However, energy is a commodity, so the best these integrated energy giants can do is react to what is taking place around them. Right now, with energy prices high, that's leading to strong financial results. However, the key issue is the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East. This highly uncertain event has upended global energy markets, leaving energy companies and entire countries in flux. Here's what Exxon, Shell, and Chevron were thinking about when they discussed earnings. The big picture: Be prepared for continued uncertainty. Exxon reported strong third-quarter 2026 earnings, with GAAP earnings of $3.72 per share, up from $1.76 a year earlier. Adjusted earnings rose from $3.52 in the second quarter of 2026 to $4.23 in the third, a jump of 20% in a single quarter.  That highlights just how volatile the energy sector is today. And the company is very clear about where that volatility is coming from, noting that "The pace of recovery in the Middle East and the broader market environment remain critical uncertainties." Essentially, that hints that the company's outlook is for elevated energy prices if the conflict continues and lower prices if the conflict draws to an end. That's not a unique perspective; Shell and Chevron pretty clearly believe the same thing. Notably, Chevron, another of the world's largest energy companies, is making a specific change to address the issue by reducing leverage. After an analyst on the company's earnings call highlighted the strength of Chevron's balance sheet, the company made a point of saying it wasn't looking to change its capital priorities. Chevron's debt-to-equity ratio is 0.17x, second only to Exxon's 0.13x. That said, Chevron, Shell, and Exxon have all been reducing leverage. A key reason for Chevron's financial prudence is its inability to predict oil price movements. Management noted that oil prices ranged from $68 to $132, a huge $64-per-barrel spread in just the third quarter. Given that backdrop, it makes complete sense that balance sheet strength remains important. And since geopolitical conflict and investor sentiment around it are key drivers of oil prices today, being prepared for volatility is really the best thing any company can do. That said, there's a changing dynamic in the global energy market that will likely linger long after the Middle East conflict ends. Shell, for example, has been in discussions with customers that range from companies to entire countries. And an increasingly important issue is energy security. Essentially, the conflict in the Middle East has increased the importance of having access to oil and natural gas that come from economically and politically stable regions. To that end, Shell highlighted that it recently gave the green light to a large expansion of a liquefied natural gas export facility in Canada. That investment, made along with project partners, will double the size of the export facility. While the project won't be complete until the early 2030s, that actually speaks to the long-term change Shell expects in the market. And management clearly highlighted on its conference call that energy security issues may lead customers to be less price-conscious. Unfortunately, there's really no clear way to know what happens next with oil prices. That's very clear when you examine what Exxon, Chevron, and Shell are saying. title: Chevron Is Doubling Venezuela Production. ExxonMobil Says It's Not in a Rush. Who's Right? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil remains cautious after Venezuela twice seized its assets. Uncertain long-term oil demand adds to investment risks. ExxonMobil's capital discipline could benefit long-term shareholders. Chevron(NYSE: CVX) plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years, potentially more than doubling its oil production there to about 600,000 barrels per day. ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), meanwhile, isn't interested in rushing back into Venezuela. And quite frankly, I think ExxonMobil may have the better strategy. Chevron isn't starting from scratch. The company has operated in Venezuela for more than a century and maintained a presence, even as political instability and economic turmoil have driven other international oil companies away. In fact, in September, Chevron announced agreements providing improved fiscal, commercial, and legal terms for its Venezuelan operations. It also secured additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Management believes it can expand production while keeping total costs below $20 per barrel. Indeed, that's a pretty attractive proposition. Chevron already has infrastructure, local relationships, and operating experience. Expanding existing production is considerably different from building an entirely new business in a country with Venezuela's history. And if oil prices remain favorable, Chevron could generate substantial additional cash flow without taking on the same level of risk as a newcomer. Exxon has good reasons to be skeptical. The company has had its Venezuelan assets seized twice, most recently in 2007 under former President Hugo Chávez. CEO Darren Woods has indicated that Exxon would consider returning, but only with stronger legal protections and investment terms that justify the risks. I don't blame him. Venezuela's oil infrastructure needs substantial investment, political uncertainty remains high, and there's no guarantee future governments will honor today's agreements. And there's also reason to consider long-term oil demand. There are varying projections on this. The IEA projects that global oil demand could plateau around 2030. Wood Mackenzie has that plateau hitting in 2032. TotalEnergies(NYSE: TTE) has it between 2035 and 2040, while OPEC suggests "robust global oil demand growth prospects to 2050, with no signs of oil demand peaking over the forecast period." But even with OPEC's optimistic scenario, 2050 is only about 23 years away. Of course, even if demand levels off, existing oil fields will continue declining. The industry will still need replacement production. But if demand growth slows while producers keep expanding capacity, oil prices could face additional pressure. Under these conditions, spending billions on politically risky projects becomes harder to justify. Chevron's expansion isn't necessarily a mistake. Its existing operations, relatively low production costs, and improved contractual terms could make Venezuela a profitable source of additional oil production. But ExxonMobil doesn't have the same advantages. It would potentially need to commit substantial capital to rebuild operations in a country that has already confiscated its assets. The company has other places to invest, including Guyana and the Permian Basin, where it has established operations and greater confidence in its ability to generate returns. Overall, ExxonMobil's strategy just makes sense. Yes, Chevron could make plenty of money in Venezuela. But ExxonMobil is demonstrating that having the financial resources to pursue an opportunity doesn't mean you should. Sometimes the better investment decision is knowing when to walk away. Exxon Mobil’s Cash Has Swung Widely But Stayed Positive Exxon’s free cash flow stayed above zero in every twelve-month stretch ending between September 2023 and September 2026, ranging from $18.8 billion to $43.0 billion. Management said that during the third quarter, conflict in the Middle East constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline, which left markets short and prices higher. Before that, Exxon’s sales had been falling. Revenue fell 4.4% in the twelve months to September 2025, after a 1.8% fall the year before. In the year to September 2025, free cash flow dropped to $23.8 billion from $32.8 billion. Exxon’s price appears to assume that much of the cash it made in 2026 will fade as the shortage eases. Management credits part of the 2026 gain to its own work, saying earlier investments that raised diesel output added $3.5 billion of margins so far in 2026, and management also counts $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019 on the way to $20 billion by 2030. Exxon’s U.S. Gulf Coast projects, starting at Baytown, are expected to raise output of distillates, such as diesel, by about 100,000 barrels a day. Management said on its call that it has no clear view of how long fuel markets will stay short. Its best guess was that markets will take until well into 2027 to get closer to normal, and possibly longer. The debt is the smaller question, since Exxon lowered its net debt by more than $9 billion in the third quarter, management said. Exxon’s cash has come through past swings with little debt ahead of its owners, but whether the higher cash of 2026 outlasts the shortage is still open. Exxon’s free cash flow in its fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch.
